pipeline_insights.text: Searching for: "cassava planting season Casamance Senegal rainy season timing"

field_chat.response:
In Casamance, the ideal cassava planting window is **June to July**, at the start of the rainy season.

**Planting:**
- Prepare land in May — clear and ridge before the first rains
- Plant stem cuttings 10–15 cm deep at a 45° angle
- Spacing: 1m × 1m (sole crop) or 2m × 0.5m with groundnut intercrop

**Recommended variety:** **TME 419** — mosaic-resistant, 12-month maturity, high starch. Available from ISRA nurseries in Ziguinchor.

**Key tip:** Weed at 3 and 8 weeks — cassava is very sensitive to early competition. Harvest April–June of the following year.

sources.title: Planting Calendar — Cassava
sources.content: Cassava planting in Casamance follows the onset of the rainy season. Optimal planting window is June-July when soil moisture is sufficient for stem cutting establishment. Late planting (August) reduces yield by 20-30% due to shorter growing season before the dry period.

sources.title: Variety Info #3 — TME 419
sources.content: TME 419 is the recommended cassava variety for the Casamance region. Developed by IITA, it shows strong resistance to cassava mosaic disease (CMD) and cassava bacterial blight (CBB). Maturity: 12 months. Yield potential: 25-35 tonnes/hectare under good management.

sources.title: Farming Calendar — Cassava
sources.content: Annual cassava farming calendar for Casamance: May - land preparation and ridging. June-July - planting. August-September - first and second weeding. October - earthing up. November-March - dry season maintenance. April-June - harvest.

sources.title: Soil Requirements — Cassava
sources.content: Cassava grows best in well-drained sandy loam soils with pH 5.5-6.5. In Casamance, the laterite soils require ridging to improve drainage. Cassava tolerates poor soils but responds well to rotation with nitrogen-fixing crops like groundnut.

sources.title: Intercropping Patterns — Cassava/Groundnut
sources.content: Cassava-groundnut intercropping is the dominant system in Casamance. Plant cassava at 2m × 0.5m spacing with groundnut rows between. The groundnut crop is harvested in October, leaving the cassava to grow through the dry season.

field_chat.image_description: Cassava leaf showing yellow and green mosaic pattern characteristic of Cassava Mosaic Disease (CMD). Leaves are distorted with irregular yellow patches interspersed with green areas. Some leaf curling visible.
field_chat.response:
This is **Cassava Mosaic Disease (CMD)** — the most common cassava disease in Casamance.

## Identification
- **Pathogen:** Cassava mosaic geminiviruses, transmitted by whitefly (*Bemisia tabaci*)
- **Confidence:** High — yellow-green mosaic pattern and leaf distortion are characteristic
- **Severity:** Moderate — clear mosaic but stems appear healthy

## Immediate Actions
1. **Do NOT uproot yet** — moderate infections still produce a harvest (30–50% yield reduction)
2. **Remove severely affected branches** — prune and burn to reduce viral load
3. **Mark this plant** — do not use its cuttings for next season

## Treatment
No chemical cure exists. Management is integrated:
- Apply **neem oil spray** (50ml neem oil + 10L water + soap) every 2 weeks to suppress whiteflies
- Remove plants with severe stunting (>70% leaf area affected)
- Next season: plant **CMD-resistant TME 419** from certified nurseries
- **Intercrop with maize** — reduces whitefly landing rates by 40–60%

sources.title: Cassava Mosaic Disease — Symptoms (Cassava)
sources.content: Cassava Mosaic Disease (CMD) is caused by a complex of geminiviruses transmitted by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci. Symptoms include yellow-green mosaic patterns on leaves, leaf distortion, and stunting. Severity ranges from mild mosaic to severe stunting with over 70% yield loss. CMD is the most economically important disease of cassava in Sub-Saharan Africa.

sources.title: Cassava Mosaic Disease — Treatment (Cassava)
sources.content: No chemical cure exists for CMD. Management relies on: (1) planting resistant varieties (TME 419, TMS 30572), (2) using clean planting material from certified sources, (3) roguing severely infected plants, (4) controlling whitefly vectors with neem-based sprays, (5) intercropping with taller crops to reduce whitefly landing. Resistant varieties reduce incidence from 60-80% to under 5%.

sources.title: Cassava Mosaic Disease — Prevention (Cassava)
sources.content: Prevention of CMD centers on breaking the infection cycle: use virus-free stem cuttings, plant resistant varieties, manage whitefly populations through intercropping and border crops, maintain field hygiene by removing and burning infected plant material. A 2-meter maize border reduces whitefly immigration by 40-60%.

sources.title: Pest Record — Whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
sources.content: Bemisia tabaci is the primary vector of cassava mosaic geminiviruses in Casamance. Population peaks during the early rainy season (June-July) when new cassava plantings are most vulnerable. Neem oil (Azadirachta indica) at 5ml/L provides effective suppression. Intercropping with maize reduces landing rates significantly.

sources.title: Variety Info #3 — TME 419
sources.content: TME 419 is the recommended cassava variety for the Casamance region. Developed by IITA, it shows strong resistance to cassava mosaic disease (CMD) and cassava bacterial blight (CBB). Maturity: 12 months. Yield potential: 25-35 tonnes/hectare under good management.

pipeline_insights.text: Searching for: "neem oil spray preparation whitefly cassava treatment"

field_chat.response:
Here's how to prepare neem oil spray for whitefly control:

## Recipe (10 liters)
- 50 ml neem oil (cold-pressed — available at Ziguinchor market)
- 10 liters clean water
- 3–5 drops liquid soap (emulsifier)

**Steps:**
1. Mix soap into a small amount of warm water
2. Add neem oil, stir vigorously until milky
3. Pour into remaining water and mix well
4. Use within 8 hours — neem degrades in sunlight

## Application
- **When:** Early morning or late afternoon
- **How:** Spray undersides of leaves — where whiteflies feed and lay eggs
- **Frequency:** Every 10–14 days during rainy season (June–October)

Neem trees are common throughout Casamance. Safe for humans, bees, and beneficial insects at these concentrations.

sources.title: Cassava Mosaic Disease — Treatment (Cassava)
sources.content: Neem oil (Azadirachta indica) at 5ml/L provides effective whitefly suppression when applied every 10-14 days. Cold-pressed neem oil is preferred for higher azadirachtin content. Add a small amount of liquid soap as an emulsifier. Apply to leaf undersides where whiteflies congregate.

sources.title: Pest Record — Whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
sources.content: Bemisia tabaci is the primary vector of cassava mosaic geminiviruses in Casamance. Population peaks during the early rainy season (June-July) when new cassava plantings are most vulnerable. Neem oil at 5ml/L provides effective suppression. Apply early morning or late afternoon to avoid rapid degradation.

sources.title: Treatment Record #7 — Neem-Based Pest Control
sources.content: Neem-based treatments are the most accessible biological pest control in Casamance. Neem trees are abundant throughout the region. Both commercial neem oil and homemade leaf extracts are effective against soft-bodied insects including whiteflies, aphids, and mealybugs. Safe for pollinators at recommended concentrations.

sources.title: Cassava Mosaic Disease — Prevention (Cassava)
sources.content: Integrated pest management for CMD vectors: combine neem sprays with cultural practices including intercropping, border crops, and field sanitation. Neem spray alone reduces whitefly populations by 60-70% but should be combined with resistant varieties for complete management.
